title: Soon ashes
hook: soon you'll be ashes; meanwhile, revere and do good (Meditations 5.33)

segments.voice: Yesterday: bad breath. Your line was it's his mouth. Which small annoyance did you forgive, or mention kindly, without anger? Day five hundred seventy-one.

Most of us flinch at the word ashes. We keep it at a distance, for funerals and a few solemn days a year. Marcus Aurelius kept it closer. In the thirty-third entry of book five he writes it in the second person, to himself, and very plainly. You'll be ashes soon. Then, in the same breath, he asks what a person should do with the time in between. His answer is short, and it isn't gloomy at all. It's a to-do list. Today: soon ashes.
screen: `WE KEEP THE WORD AT A DISTANCE.` → `MARCUS KEPT IT CLOSE.` → `SOON ASHES.`

segments.voice: First, the fact. Soon, very soon, Marcus writes, you'll be ashes, or a skeleton, and either a name or not even a name. And a name is only a sound and an echo. Second, the squabbling. Then he looks at what people spend their lives fighting over. The things most prized in life, he says, are empty and small: puppies snapping at each other, children quarreling, laughing, and then crying a minute later. He even borrows a phrase from the Greek poet Hesiod, about virtues fleeing the wide earth for Olympus, and applies it to faithfulness, modesty, justice and truth. It's a wry picture of a world that often forgets what matters. Third, so what's holding you here? Marcus asks himself what keeps him attached to any of it, since the things we sense are always changing and our own senses are easily fooled. His answer is to wait calmly for the end, whatever it turns out to be. Fourth, meanwhile. And until then, what's enough? Here's the list. To revere the gods and speak well of them, Marcus says. To do good to people. To bear with them, and to hold back. And to remember that whatever lies outside your own small flesh and breath is not yours and not up to you. Notice the word meanwhile. Marcus doesn't use ashes to stop himself from living. He uses it to clear the desk. The squabbles drop off. What's left fits on a card: reverence, kindness, patience, restraint. For him, reverence meant the gods of Stoic belief. Readers on many paths keep that part in their own words, or in none. The rest is open to anyone: do good, now, while there's a now.
screen: `SOON ASHES, AND A NAME, OR NOT EVEN.` · `PUPPIES SNAPPING, CHILDREN QUARRELING.` · `WHAT HOLDS YOU HERE?` · `MEANWHILE: REVERE, DO GOOD, BEAR.` · then, large: `MEANWHILE, DO GOOD.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Say the word quietly to yourself: ashes. Let it be plain, not frightening. Now feel your breath, warm and still here. Meanwhile. Bring to mind one good act you could do right now, or within the hour: a message, a kindness, a bit of patience with someone. Small is fine. Decide on it. When the bell ends, do it. The bell holds the time.
Soon ashes. Marcus reminds himself he'll soon be ashes and a name; meanwhile, it's enough to revere, to do good, and to bear with people. Today's word.
Your line: meanwhile, do good. Do one good act now, before anything else on your list. Day five hundred seventy-one.

howItsDone: Readers of Marcus Aurelius sometimes use the plain reminder of Meditations 5.33, 'soon ashes', to clear away small quarrels and do one good act right away.

original.note: Greek, 'ashes': the plain word Marcus uses for what he will soon be.

trapdoor: what you thought: life is short, so stop wasting it.
what it means: the thought of ashes clears away the squabbles, and leaves a short list: reverence, kindness, patience, restraint.

what a scholar hears: Marcus borrows a phrase from Hesiod's Works and Days, where Shame and Retribution leave the earth, and fits his own four virtues to it, placing his age inside an old Greek story of decline.

notes: 5.33 paraphrased: soon, very soon, you will be ashes or a skeleton, and either a name or not even a name; a name is sound and echo; the things much valued in life are empty, rotten, trifling, like little dogs biting one another, little children quarreling, laughing, then crying; fidelity, modesty, justice and truth are fled 'Up to Olympus from the wide-spread earth' (Hesiod); what then detains you here? wait in tranquility for the end, whether extinction or removal elsewhere; until then, what is sufficient? to venerate the gods and bless them, to do good to men, to practice tolerance and self-restraint; and to remember that what is beyond the limits of the poor flesh and breath is neither yours nor in your power. Confirm.
Hesiod, Works and Days c. 197–201 (Aidos and Nemesis leaving the earth); Marcus's list of four virtues may be his adaptation. Confirm line reference and wording of the paraphrase.
The line 'For him, reverence meant the gods of Stoic belief. Readers on many paths keep that part in their own words, or in none' describes without prescribing; confirm tone.

Teach, match, myth and trapdoor revised so Hesiod is credited only with the phrase about leaving the wide earth for Olympus (Works and Days 197–200, of Aidos and Nemesis), not with Marcus's list of four virtues.
